## Bernoulli Random Variable

::: {.callout title="Definition 14.1"}
A **Bernoulli distribution** models the outcome of a binary experiment (success or failure), when the probability of success is $p$. The PMF for a Bernoulli random variable is:

$$
P(X = x) = P_X(x;p) = p^x (1 - p)^{1 - x}, \quad x \in \{0, 1\}
$$

and the CDF is:

$$
F_X(x;p) = 
P(X \leq x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & x < 0 \\
1 - p & 0 \leq x < 1 \\
1 & x \geq 1
\end{cases}
$$

The mean $\text{E}[X]$ and variance $\text{Var}[X]$ are:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= p \\
\text{Var}[X] &= p(1-p)
\end{align}
$$
:::

## Bernoulli Mean and Variance

The mean of a Bernoulli random variable is derived as follows:

$$
\text{E}[X] = \sum_{x=0}^{1} x \cdot P_X(x) = 0 \cdot (1-p) + 1 \cdot p = p
$$

and the variance is derived in a similar manner:

$$
\text{Var}[X] = (0 - p)^2 \cdot (1-p) + (1 - p)^2 \cdot p = p(1 - p)
$$

## Ex: Coin Toss

::: {.callout title="Example 14.1"}
You are playing a game where you flip a weighted coin and win if it comes up heads. The probability it comes up heads is 0.6. Answer the following:

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 1)$, and $P(X \leq 1)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = 0.6$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = 0.6 \times 0.4 = 0.24$
-   $P(X = 1) = 0.6$
-   $P(X \leq 1) = 1$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.6
dbinom(x = 1, size = 1, prob = p)
pbinom(q = 1, size = 1, prob = p)
```

## Ex: Dice Roll

::: {.callout title="Example 14.2"}
You are playing a game where you roll a fair six-sided die and win if it comes up a 1 or a 6. Let $X$ be a random variable that is 1 if you win and 0 otherwise.

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 1)$, and $P(X \leq 0.5)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = \frac{1}{3}$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{2}{9}$
-   $P(X = 1) = \frac{1}{3}$
-   $P(X \leq 0.5) = \frac{2}{3}$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 1/3
dbinom(x = 1, size = 1, prob = p)
pbinom(q = 0.5, size = 1, prob = p)
```

## Binomial Random Variable

::: {.callout title="Definition 14.2"}
A **Binomial distribution** models the number of successful outcomes in a total of $n$ trials where each trial has a probability of success $p$. In other words, it is the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli random variables. The PMF for a Binomial random variable is:

$$
P(X = x) = P_X(x;n,p) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1 - p)^{n - x}, \quad x \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots, n\}
$$

and the CDF is:

$$
F_X(x;n,p) = 
P(X \leq x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & x < 0 \\
\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor x \rfloor} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k} & 0 \leq x \leq n \\
1 & x > n
\end{cases}
$$

The mean $\text{E}[X]$ and variance $\text{Var}[X]$ are:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= np \\
\text{Var}[X] &= np(1-p)
\end{align}
$$
:::

## Binomial Random Variable

```{r}
# Set parameters
n <- 20  # Number of trials
p_values <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)  # Different probabilities of success

# Create a data frame to store the binomial probabilities
binom_data <- data.frame()

for (p in p_values) {
  x <- 0:n
  prob <- dbinom(x, size = n, prob = p)
  binom_data <- rbind(binom_data, data.frame(x = x, prob = prob, p = factor(p)))
}

# Plot the binomial distributions
ggplot(binom_data, aes(x = x, y = prob, color = p, group = p)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Binomial Distributions with Different p Values",
       x = "Number of Successes",
       y = "Probability",
       color = "p") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Binomial Mean and Variance

The mean of a Binomial random variable is derived as follows:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= \sum_{x=1}^{n} x \frac{n!}{x!(n-x)!} p^x (1 - p)^{n - x} \\
&= \sum_{x=1}^{n} \frac{n!}{(x-1)!(n-x)!} p^x (1 - p)^{n - x} & \text{Let } y=x-1 \text{ and } m=n-1 \\
&= \sum_{y=0}^m \frac{(m+1)!}{y!(m-y)!}p^{y+1}(1-p)^{m-y} \\
&= (m+1)p \sum_{y=0}^m \frac{m!}{y!(m-y)!}p^y(1-p)^{m-y} & \text{Binomial PMF sums to 1} \\
&= (m+1)p = np
\end{align}
$$

The variance could be derived in a similar way by first finding $\text{E}[X(X-1)]$.

## Ex: Coin Tosses

::: {.callout title="Example 14.4"}
You flip a weighted coin 10 times where the probability of a head is 0.4 each time. Let $X$ be the number of heads.

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 4)$, and $P(X \leq 5)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = 10 \times 0.4 = 4$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = 10 \times 0.4 \times 0.6 = 2.4$
-   $P(X = 4) = \binom{10}{4} 0.4^4 \times 0.6^6 \simeq 0.2508$
-   $P(X \leq 5) = \sum_{k=0}^5 \binom{10}{k} 0.4^k \times 0.6^{10-k} \simeq 0.8338$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 10
p <- 0.4
dbinom(x = 4, size = n, prob = p)
pbinom(q = 5, size = n, prob = p)
```

## Ex: Rocket Launches

::: {.callout title="Example 14.5"}
A company knows that the probability of a successful rocket launch is 0.75. The company is going to launch 20 rockets in a year. Let $X$ be the number of successful launches.

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 15)$, and $P(X < 16)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = 20 \times 0.75 = 15$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = 20 \times 0.75 \times 0.25 = 3.75$
-   $P(X = 15) = \binom{20}{15} 0.75^{15} \times 0.25^5 \simeq 0.2023$
-   $P(X < 16) = \sum_{k=0}^{15} \binom{20}{k} 0.75^k \times 0.25^{10-k} \simeq 0.5852$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 20
p <- 0.75
dbinom(x = 15, size = n, prob = p)
pbinom(q = 15, size = n, prob = p)
```

## Poisson Random Variable

::: {.callout title="Definition 14.3"}
A **Poisson distribution** models the number of occurrences of an event when the events are independent and occur at a constant rate ($\lambda$). This could be the number of occurrences in a given period of time or a given metric space. The PMF for a Poisson random variable is:

$$
P(X = x) = P_X(x;\lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}, \quad x \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}
$$

and the CDF is:

$$
F_X(x;\lambda) = 
P(X \leq x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & x < 0 \\
\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor x \rfloor} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!} & x \geq 0
\end{cases}
$$

The mean $\text{E}[X]$ and variance $\text{Var}[X]$ are:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= \lambda \\
\text{Var}[X] &= \lambda
\end{align}
$$
:::

## Poisson Random Variable

```{r}
# Set parameters
lambda_values <- c(1, 4, 10)  # Different values of lambda

# Create a data frame to store the Poisson probabilities
poisson_data <- data.frame()

for (lambda in lambda_values) {
  x <- 0:(max(lambda_values) * 2)  # Set x-range based on the largest lambda
  prob <- dpois(x, lambda = lambda)
  poisson_data <- rbind(poisson_data, data.frame(x = x, prob = prob, lambda = factor(lambda)))
}

# Plot the Poisson distributions
ggplot(poisson_data, aes(x = x, y = prob, color = lambda, group = lambda)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Poisson Distributions with Different Lambda Values",
       x = "Number of Events",
       y = "Probability",
       color = expression(lambda)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Poisson Mean and Variance

The mean of a Poisson random variable is derived as follows:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= \sum_{x=1}^{\infty} x \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!} \\
&= \sum_{x=1}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{(x-1)!} & \text{Let } y = x-1 \\
&= \sum_{y=0}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y+1}}{y!} \\
&= \lambda \sum_{y=0}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!} = \lambda & \text{Poisson PMF sums to 1}
\end{align}
$$

The variance could be derived in a similar way by first finding $\text{E}[X(X-1)]$.

## Ex: Call Center

::: {.callout title="Example 14.7"}
On average, a call center receives 3 calls per minute. Let $X$ be the number of calls received in a given minute.

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 5)$, and $P(X \leq 2)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = 3$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = 3$
-   $P(X = 5) = \frac{e^{-3}3^5}{5!} \simeq 0.1008$
-   $P(X \leq 2) = \sum_{k=0}^{2} \frac{e^{-3}3^k}{k!} \simeq 0.4232$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
lambda <- 3
dpois(x = 5, lambda = lambda)
ppois(q = 2, lambda = lambda)
```

## Ex: Potholes

::: {.callout title="Example 14.8"}
On average, there are 4 potholes in a mile stretch of road. Let $X$ be the number of potholes on a mile stretch of road.

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 2)$, and $P(X \geq 4)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = 4$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = 4$
-   $P(X = 2) = \frac{e^{-4}4^2}{2!} \simeq 0.1465$
-   $P(X \geq 4) = 1-P(X \leq 3) = 1-\sum_{k=0}^{3} \frac{e^{-4}4^k}{k!} \simeq 0.5665$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
lambda <- 4
dpois(x = 2, lambda = lambda)
1-ppois(q = 3, lambda = lambda)
```

## Geometric Random Variable

::: {.callout title="Definition 14.4"}
A **Geometric distribution** models the number of failures in a sequence of independent trials before a success occurs with the probability of success being $p$ each time. The PMF for a Geometric random variable is:

$$
P(X = x) = P_X(x;p) = p(1-p)^x, \quad x \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}
$$

and the CDF is:

$$
F_X(x;p) = 
P(X \leq x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & x < 0 \\
1-(1-p)^{\lfloor x \rfloor+1} & x \geq 0
\end{cases}
$$

The mean $\text{E}[X]$ and variance $\text{Var}[X]$ are:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= \frac{1-p}{p}\\
\text{Var}[X] &= \frac{1-p}{p^2}
\end{align}
$$
:::

## Geometric Random Variable

```{r}
# Set parameters
p_values <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)  # Different probabilities of success

# Create a data frame to store the geometric probabilities
geom_data <- data.frame()

for (p in p_values) {
  x <- 0:15  # Number of failures before the first success
  prob <- dgeom(x, prob = p)
  geom_data <- rbind(geom_data, data.frame(x = x, prob = prob, p = factor(p)))
}

# Plot the geometric distributions
ggplot(geom_data, aes(x = x, y = prob, color = p, group = p)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Geometric Distributions with Different p Values",
       x = "Number of Failures Before First Success",
       y = "Probability",
       color = "p") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Geometric Mean and Variance

The mean of a geometric random variable is derived as follows:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= \sum_{x=0}^{\infty} x p(1-p)^x \\
&= p(p-1) \sum_{x=0}^{\infty} \frac{-1}{(1-p)} x(1-p)^x & \text{Multiplied by 1} \\
&= p(p-1) \sum_{x=0}^{\infty} \frac{d}{dp}(1-p)^x \\
&= p(p-1) \frac{d}{dp} \sum_{x=0}^{\infty} (1-p)^x & \text{Derivative of convergent series} \\
&= p(p-1) \frac{d}{dp} \frac{1}{p} = \frac{1-p}{p} & \text{Convergence of geometric series}
\end{align}
$$

The variance could be derived in a similar way by first finding $\text{E}[X(X-1)]$.

## Ex: Coin Flips

::: {.callout title="Example 14.10"}
A certain coin has a probability 0.2 of coming up heads. Let $X$ be the number of tails you get until you get your first head.

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 6)$, and $P(X > 8)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = \frac{0.8}{0.2} = 4$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = \frac{0.8}{0.2^2} = 20$
-   $P(X = 6) = 0.2 \times 0.8^6 \simeq 0.0524$
-   $P(X > 8) = 1-P(X \leq 8) = 1-\left[1-(1-0.2)^{8+1} \right] \simeq 0.1342$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.2
dgeom(x = 6, prob = p)
1-pgeom(q = 8, prob = p)
```

## Ex: Deck of Cards

::: {.callout title="Example 14.11"}
You play a game where you draw cards with replacement from a standard deck of 52 cards until you get a face card. Let $X$ be the number of non face-cards drawn before you draw a face card.

What are $\text{E}[X]$, $\text{Var}[X]$, $P(X = 10)$, and $P(X \leq 10)$?
:::

. . .

-   $\text{E}[X] = \frac{1-0.2308}{0.2308} = 3.33$
-   $\text{Var}[X] = \frac{1-0.2308}{0.2308^2} = 14.44$
-   $P(X = 10) = 0.2308 \times 0.7692^{10} \simeq 0.0167$
-   $P(X \leq 10) = 1-(1-0.2308)^{10+1} \simeq 0.9442$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 12/52
dgeom(x = 10, prob = p)
pgeom(q = 10, prob = p)
```
